9.0.s.en: (1) Paul's sorrow over the unbelief of the Jews

9.0.0.en: In this chapter St. Paul declares the extent of his love and zeal for the salvation of the Jews who did not believe, saying, with all the sincerity flowing from his union with Christ, and with the witness of both his conscience and the Holy Spirit, that he does not lie when he says that he is very sorrowful from the depths of his heart because of the unbelief of many of the Jews in Christ.

9.1.0.en: Paul wishes the salvation of the Jews even if it were at the cost of himself, as Moses did long ago in his intercession for the children of Israel when they sinned, and Moses said to God, "Yet now, if thou wilt forgive their sin; and if not, blot me, I pray thee, out of thy book which thou hast written" (Ex 32:32). The words of St. Paul should not be taken literally, for he certainly does not wish to be cut off from Christ, of whom he said in the previous chapter, "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ?" Rather, he said these words to clear himself of the charge that he had sacrificed them and disowned them as his people, his kinsmen, and his relatives according to the flesh after his faith in Christ; indeed, he shows his self-giving love toward them because he was moved by the love of Christ the Redeemer on the Cross.

9.2.0.en: Paul does not forget the great privileges with which God singled them out above all other peoples, for they are:

9.2.1.en: Israelites: the title Jacob received from God so that his offspring might become a people special to Him. To them pertaineth the adoption: "Ye are the children of the Lord your God" (Deut 14:1). And the glory: the only people in the world who saw the glory of God in the form of the pillars of cloud and fire in the wilderness and in the tabernacle.

9.2.2.en: The covenants: how many covenants of love God made with them, yet, what a wonder, they turned back from their covenants with God.

9.2.3.en: The giving of the law: the Law that revealed God's will and disciplined man.

9.2.4.en: The service of God: He taught them how to worship God with prayer, rites, and the offering of sacrifices. The promises: those connected with the coming of the Messiah, the Savior of the world.

9.3.0.en: The fathers: they are Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, beloved of God.

9.3.1.en: And more important than all that precedes is the coming of the Lord Christ from their offspring, from the flesh of the Virgin Mary, yet He is not an ordinary man but an eternal, everlasting God, to whom be all glory and blessing forever, Amen.

9.3.2.en: If God has granted you circumstances that help you in the spiritual life, make use of them and enjoy your sonship to God, lest if you neglect them they condemn you on the last day. Seize every opportunity and respond to the voice of God today in order to draw near to Him.

9.4.s.en: (2) God's promise to the elect only

9.4.0.en: Perhaps some think that the word of God has failed, that is, God's promise of the salvation of the people of Israel.

9.4.1.en: So Paul denied that, affirming that the word of God and His promises are firm and do not fail through the ages. For God's promise is only for the true, spiritual Israelite who will be joined to Christ the promised Savior, who is the goal of the Old Testament, and not for all the children of Abraham according to the flesh, as proved by the fact that Ishmael is a son of Abraham according to the flesh but did not receive the promise; rather the promise is fulfilled through Isaac, who would keep the faith firm like his father until Christ came, who is the goal of the promise and the blessing to Abraham.

9.5.0.en: Sonship is fundamentally sonship to God, and the condition of sonship to God is not sonship to Abraham according to the flesh, but faith and holding fast to God's promises, that is, faith in Christ.

9.6.0.en: When He promised Sarah that she would have a son in her old age, Sarah became a vessel for raising up the offspring of God.

9.7.0.en: To affirm that God's choice is not limited to fleshly descent, St. Paul gave a strong example in Jacob and Esau, the twins from the womb of Rebecca, the wife of our father Isaac, who were alike in father and mother.

9.8.0.en: Here God did not choose both, but by His foreknowledge looked at the future of each of them and found Jacob, the younger, more loving toward Him and more careful to please Him than his brother, so God chose him although Jacob's works were not perfect, for he fell into the sins of deceit and lying. And the phrase (not of works) means that however much a person's works attain of righteousness, he has not yet reached the degree of deserving God's choice of him, but the choice is a gift and an overflowing grace from God who loves mankind who respond to Him, to support them and raise them to His perfection.

9.9.0.en: Although Esau was the elder, God chose Jacob, and he became lord over Esau, because he was better qualified to inherit the virtues and blessing of Isaac his father.

9.10.0.en: So God's love for Jacob came not as partiality from God toward him, but because He had foreseen him to be worthy of this love. Jacob's good works came afterward, confirming the exactness of God's choice of him, and as a simple offering from Jacob to the loving God, while God's hatred of Esau was not an injustice to him but based on God's foreknowledge that Esau was a hard-hearted man who made light of grace.

9.10.1.en: And also, not everyone in the Church is elect, for the Church, like Rebecca, bears the chosen person and the rejected person. So be careful, beloved, to be among the elect who please God's heart by your obedience to His commandments.

9.11.0.en: Certainly God is not unjust, and God's choosing of one person and not another never means that God has determined eternal bliss for some and eternal destruction for others, otherwise man would not be responsible for his life; but the truth is that God's choice is based on His foreknowledge of man's heart, conduct, works, and all the details of his life.

9.11.1.en: So the conclusion is that God chooses the person who wants to choose God.

9.12.0.en: Therefore God said to Moses: with all my esteem for man in his striving and his works, this does not mean that the heavenly gifts man receives are the price of this striving, but they are an invaluable grace granted certainly to those who strive and withheld from the slack. Therefore God said, "I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I will have compassion," because all the credit in grace goes back to my mercy and compassion, and consequently it is not Israel's right to be angry because of my choosing the Gentiles, for my mercy and compassion, based on my foreknowledge, belong to me alone as God.

9.13.0.en: "Not of him that willeth": does not mean that God gives no weight to the human will and human striving by good works, but its meaning is that man by his will and striving is unable to reach a good enough level to deserve compassion and mercy, and that the doing of good is among the mercies of God's grace supporting human helplessness, as the Lord Christ said, "without me ye can do nothing" (Jn 15:5). Therefore the result came: not of him that willeth, but of God that sheweth mercy.

9.13.1.en: Do not persist in an evil in your heart, however many good works you have, for they will not profit you. You must purify your heart by repentance and forgiveness so that you may be saved.

9.14.0.en: When God wanted to deliver His people Israel from the land of Egypt, He chose Pharaoh, hard-hearted and resisting God, to show God's longsuffering in bearing Pharaoh's delay and stubbornness throughout the period of the ten plagues. And He chose Moses, the meek, and raised and glorified him, to deliver the people from the hand of Pharaoh. The phrase "whom he will he hardeneth" means that God allowed Pharaoh to show the hardness that was already in him and to defy God, but if God had willed, He would have destroyed Pharaoh from the first plague, yet He left him in his hardness time after time so that God might be glorified in the end.

9.15.0.en: Some misunderstood the preceding verse and thought that God toys with human hearts, putting mercy in some and hardness in others against their will, and consequently He has no right to blame anyone, as though man were driven and not free to choose.

9.16.0.en: Here St. Paul returns to speaking to the Jews, who denied God's right to bring the Gentiles into the fold of faith. St. Paul replies to them sharply, "Who art thou, O Jew, that repliest against God?" God's will, His desire, and His mercy are matters that belong to Him alone and are at the very heart of His work as God, who has all power, depth of thought, and perfection of justice in His choices, and no person has the right to call God to account, because the creature has no right to judge the Creator, since his understanding counts as nothing before God's unlimited wisdom.

9.16.1.en: You have the right to speak with God with all that is in your heart with the innocence of a child, and be confident that He loves you and wants to hear your voice. Only humble yourself before Him and speak as you wish even if you express yourself wrongly, for He will guide you because He is your tender Father.

9.17.0.en: Paul cited the parable of the potter who has absolute authority over one lump of clay to make of it a vessel unto honor, like a beautiful work of art, or a vessel unto dishonor, like a flowerpot.

9.18.0.en: The vessels of wrath is Pharaoh, hard-hearted from the beginning, perishing in all cases; God used him as a visual aid to show His wrath against the wicked and the power of His vengeance on them, by drowning Pharaoh and the Egyptians in the Red Sea, after He had endured him throughout the period of the ten plagues. We note that St. Paul did not say that God is the one who made the vessels of wrath, but only that He endured them, because man by his own evil becomes a vessel that angers God.

9.19.0.en: The vessels of mercy is Israel, humiliated from slavery in the land of Egypt, whom He took to the Promised Land, and they became a people of consequence, and He made for them a great name, glorified among the peoples, and here the greatness of God's mercy toward them appeared. And so God does with many who appear persecuted and humiliated in the world for His name's sake, but He supports them and then glorifies them in heaven.

9.20.0.en: As God chose the wretched Jews to have mercy on them, so also His mercy extended to include the wretched Gentiles, to make of them His people, that is, the Church of the New Testament, side by side with Christians of Jewish origin.

9.21.0.en: The matter of God's choosing the Gentiles is not a new matter to the Jews, because many prophecies of the Old Testament spoke about the entrance of the Gentiles into the Church, such as Hosea (2:23), who said that the Gentiles who were not of the people of God became His people, and those who were hated became beloved.

9.22.0.en: The peoples and places that previously refused to worship God have become children of God.

9.22.1.en: The Church teaches us never to judge anyone as lost, however sinful, until he dies. For today's sinner may be tomorrow's saint, and the reverse is true. Nor do we hasten to declare a person's holiness except after his repose and the Church's assurance of the truthfulness of his life. So offer prayers for every person who sins, and show him your love more than to the righteous believers.

9.23.0.en: As for Israel, the people numerous as the sand of the sea, they rejected Christ, but at the end of days some of the Jews will believe in the Lord Christ and be saved (Isa 10:22).

9.24.0.en: Finishing the work: God will prolong His longsuffering until He accomplishes His purpose and His love in the salvation of some of the Jews at the end of days.

9.24.1.en: Cutting it short in righteousness: God is like any just ruler who will judge in righteousness the Jews who will believe at the end of days. Left us a seed: the remnant who will believe from among the Jews at the end of days.

9.24.2.en: God will continue to call the Jews to faith until the end of days, and a number whom He calls a little seed will believe in Him, and for the sake of these He is longsuffering toward the people of Israel to this day, and has not destroyed them like the people of Sodom and Gomorrah (Isa 1:9). This declares that there is a number of Jews who will believe in Christ although many of them have refused faith.

9.24.3.en: Do you not notice with me, beloved, the longsuffering and compassion of God? He is the one who endured Pharaoh many times, and was patient with the people of Israel for about 2000 years, and so He is patient with us to give us every opportunity for repentance, so that even if we are hard-hearted we may be ashamed before His love and hasten to Him in repentance.

9.25.s.en: (4) The reason for the Gentiles' justification and the Jews' stumbling

9.25.0.en: The Gentiles, who lived in the darkness of spiritual ignorance and did not walk in the way of the works of the Law, have now arrived at justification by faith; while the people of Israel, who spent their whole lives seeking to carry out the Law in every letter, did not perceive the depth of the law of righteousness and that it leads to reaching Christ, and the result was that they did not obtain true righteousness.

9.26.0.en: St. Paul gives the reason why Israel did not attain righteousness, which is that it did not seek righteousness by faith in Christ, but sought it as a price it deserved as a natural result of its walking by the works of the Law, so the Israelites stumbled at a stone, who is the Lord Christ, who exposed their hypocrisy and rejected their self-righteousness and pride, and so all they did was to crucify Him and kill Him and deny His resurrection.

9.27.0.en: St. Paul cited the book of Isaiah (Isa 8:14) in support of his words, that the Jews who rejected Christ stumbled at Him, so they fell and went out from the fold of faith. But whoever trusts in the Lord Christ, the Rock of ages, the cornerstone, and the foundation of the Church, shall not be ashamed and will not be exposed to eternal shame in the judgment.

9.27.1.en: Therefore let us bow down in thanksgiving to our God, who came to us with His righteousness, and counted us as vessels of mercy, chose us and had compassion on us, and made us vessels unto honor and glory according to His will. But we, beloved, must remain firm in this choice, or we too will be rejected, as Israel was rejected because of the hardness of its heart.

9.27.2.en: And all this does not nullify or abolish the place and importance of the Law in the Old Testament; rather the Law, like a great commander, now retires and hands over the command to the new Commander, our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be all glory and honor. The Jews' rejection of faith and the Gentiles' acceptance of it

10.0.s.en: (1) The Jews seek their own righteousness

10.0.0.en: St. Paul declares that the desire of his heart, his delight, and his prayers are for the salvation of Israel, for his heart is torn with pain, sorrow, and grief over the children of Israel who rejected Christ and so were rejected by God.

10.1.0.en: Here is St. Paul, with an eye of pure love that does not criticize, looking at the one sweet advantage in the Jews, which is their intense holding to God and their zeal for His name, though it lacks spiritual knowledge, remembering himself personally when he was very zealous for God; in his ignorance he persecuted the Christians before his heart was enlightened by the vision of Christ.

10.2.0.en: The righteousness of God: the work of the merciful God in the believer's life to justify him, as a gift to submissive, humble believers.

10.2.1.en: The Jews in their pride ignored the righteousness of Christ and wanted to prove their worthiness by justifying themselves by their works, to take all the glory and praise for their swollen selves, and the result was that they did not obtain righteousness because of their pride.

10.3.0.en: The Jews were ignorant that the whole aim of the Law, the sacrifices, and the Old Testament is to prepare mankind to receive Christ, who gives righteousness to everyone who believes in Him.

10.4.0.en: St. Paul returns to convince the Jews of the impossibility of justification by the Law, because Moses laid down a condition, which is that man do all the works of the Law and not err in a single one of them in order to receive justification and so live. But who of mankind can do that?!

10.4.1.en: Would that you looked at people's virtues and not at their faults to condemn them. And know that no person, however wicked, can be without virtues. If you train your eyes to discover people's virtues, that is, to praise them, you will give rest to your heart and benefit from these virtues, and at the same time win the love of others, and then you will look at their faults with an eye of compassion and find excuses for them and pray for them.

10.5.s.en: (2) The righteousness of Christ is available to every person

10.5.0.en: "Who shall ascend into heaven?": So people asked in the Old Testament, since they saw righteousness high and far from them like heaven, and they said: is there a person who can rise to heaven and live righteousness?! That is, there is not one righteous person who can fulfill the Law.

10.5.1.en: "To bring Christ down": People wished for and awaited the Messiah the Savior and said in the Old Testament: who will rise to heaven to bring us the Christ who gives us righteousness?

10.5.2.en: Justification by faith has now become possible, after the spiritual life had been as far from man as heaven is from earth, but the Lord Christ by His Incarnation brought the spiritual world and the heavenly things down to us on earth, into our hearts and our Church.

10.6.0.en: Christ offered us redemption on a silver platter, when He died and then went down to Hades to free the captives in it, and then rose from the dead without any effort from you and without anyone asking you to go down to Hades to raise Him. This is in comparison with the exhausting efforts required of the believer in the Old Testament, of offering sacrifices..... and so on.

10.6.1.en: And all you have to do is to believe in His resurrection and in the power of His justification, and not be like the Jews who denied His resurrection, saying, "Who can bring Christ up from Hades?"

10.6.2.en: For the Jews were unable to understand the work of the Messiah, how He would come up from the Hades to which He went down, to bring up those who died in hope, and they forgot that He is God, able to raise Himself and to raise with Him all who died in hope.

10.6.3.en: Yes, beloved, salvation has become within reach through Christ Jesus. Shall we not make use of this opportunity while we are alive on earth, lest the time pass us by? That is by repentance and partaking of the Holy Mysteries, which results in being concerned with speaking with God in prayer and reading His word in the Holy Bible every day.

10.7.0.en: By our confession of Christ, but not an oral confession. The Christian of old used to confess Christ with the sword at his neck, but let us confess Christ at least:

10.7.1.en: a- By our good conduct and our outward behavior, so that we bear witness that we are children of God.

10.7.2.en: b- By our faith of the heart that the God who raised Christ from the dead is able to raise us from all our falls, so that our inner life is purified and thus we are saved.

10.8.0.en: So the person who is sanctified by his conduct and his heart receives righteousness and salvation.

10.9.0.en: All who believed receive victory over their sins and glory and honor in eternity.

10.10.0.en: Since the Jew and the Greek (the Gentile) are equal in their sins before God, so everyone who calls upon the name of the Lord, whether Jew or Greek, is equal in receiving righteousness from the one God, rich in His generosity and giving to mankind.

10.11.0.en: For everyone who makes Christ his God (calls upon the name of the Lord) by faith will be saved, and why? Because he has become one with Christ, and has the resurrection and life of Christ, who is the only way to salvation. Of course this does not mean that salvation is by mere general faith in God - that is, as in any religion, as the Catholic Church claims in the heresy of "the universality of salvation" - but salvation has conditions set by the Holy Bible.

10.11.1.en: How great is the generosity of our Lord Jesus Christ, who does not look at faces but at the heart. The world divides people into positions and ranks, rich and poor. A mother may discriminate among her children by partiality, but in Christ Jesus all people have equal opportunities to obtain salvation. So do not be distressed by your weaknesses and shortcomings, for Christ loves you and is ready to supply all your needs and give you complete joy.

10.12.s.en: (3) The Jews' rejection of the preaching

10.12.0.en: For any person to call on the name of the Lord, that is, to pray to Christ and consider Him God, he must first believe in Him, and that is after he hears about Him through a preacher (evangelist).

10.13.0.en: For the preachers to succeed in their mission, they must be sent from God in the name of the Lord Christ by the grace and help of the Holy Spirit. Isaiah (Isa 52:7) had earlier blessed their weary feet and described them as bringing glad tidings of peace, good things, salvation, and freedom from sin. They are not like the prophets of the Old Testament who carried threats and warnings, while the glad tidings were postponed until Christ came.

10.13.1.en: We ask ourselves as servants: does peace show in our lives so that everyone is drawn to our Christ who gives peace, or do the worries and desires of the world appear in us?!

10.14.0.en: It was supposed that the Jews would be the first to believe the news, and even to take part themselves in preaching Christ like the rest of the apostles, but instead they did not believe the good news of the Gospel but resisted it, and Isaiah had earlier prophesied about them (Isa 53:1), saying, "Who hath believed our report?" from Israel, that is, the preaching of Christ.

10.15.0.en: Faith is accomplished by believing the report and the Incarnation and redemption of Christ, who is the Word of God, and therefore whoever rejects the report rejects God Himself.

10.16.0.en: The Israelites are responsible for their rejection, and they have no argument that they did not hear the report, because the preaching of Christ reached all the regions of the inhabited world through the apostles, and also through the Jews gathered on the day of Pentecost from all the countries of the world. These, when they learned the news of the resurrection of Christ, believed, and then each went off to his country to carry the glad tidings to his Jewish relatives scattered throughout the world.

10.17.0.en: Certainly Israel knew the news of the Gospel and rejected it by their own will. Here St. Paul cites two great prophets, Moses and Isaiah, who prophesied about Israel's rejection of faith in Christ. First, Moses prophesied in Deuteronomy (32:21) that God would reject them as His people and provoke them to jealousy by accepting the Gentiles, whom He called of old "a foolish nation" in regard to spiritual matters. And if the Gentiles understood God's wisdom, what excuse have the Jews for not understanding, they who are the intelligent?

10.17.1.en: Second, God spoke through Isaiah (65:1), saying: I, as God, have become understood and clear to those who did not seek me or ask about me, that is, the Gentiles.

10.17.2.en: Here a person outside the Church may hear about Christ, and his heart is filled with love for Him, and he offers strong repentance and a new holy life more than an outwardly religious and inwardly proud person. So do not rely on your habit of attachment to the Church, but let there be inward repentance in you and an effort to understand what you pray and hear.

10.18.0.en: But as for Israel, "All day long I have stretched forth my hands," I, God, in love to them (throughout the period of the Old Testament) through the calling of the prophets. But as for them, their hearts turned to stone and they resisted me and were stubborn toward me. The phrase "stretched forth my hands" is a reference to the Cross of Christ, where He was stretching out (opening) His arms to mankind, stubborn and refusing His salvation, that perhaps it might repent.

10.18.1.en: The faith of the Jews before the end of days
